1.1 Software Bid

The Enhanced Personal Finance Analyzer is an academic desktop solution for recording personal income and expenditure, planning category budgets, and tracking savings goals. The proposed benefit is a single local view of manually entered financial activity, with immediate explanatory feedback before an expense is recorded. It does not initiate payments or synchronize bank accounts.

The problem is fragmentation of everyday records across cash, digital payment descriptions and informal notes. A monthly total alone does not show which category dominates discretionary spending or how a proposed purchase affects a budget. This project addresses those questions through categorized records, monthly aggregation and transparent financial rules.
Scope of work and technical approach

The final scope includes local account authentication, transaction maintenance, custom categories, monthly category limits, ratio-based savings allocation, recurring-entry catch-up, charts, text reports, and file transfer functions. JavaFX presents forms and tables; Java services apply validation and calculations; JDBC accesses a local SQLite database. Monetary values use BigDecimal in Java and integer paise in storage.

rows: Java 21, JavaFX, Maven and SQLite are identified in pom.xml and source.

items.text: This bid is a retrospective academic statement of the delivered scope, not evidence of a commercial tender, quoted fee or client acceptance. Calendar commitments and role allocations have not been reconstructed without records.
Source evidence: pom.xml; app/MainApp.java:init(); dao/jdbc/DatabaseManager.java:initializeDatabase()

The application organizes a financial workflow around tracking, planning and analysis. Tracking creates a categorized history. Planning compares actual spending with monthly limits and records progress toward selected goals. Analysis presents aggregate indicators and rule-triggered observations. The user remains responsible for entering accurate records and deciding how to act on the advice.

Intended users include students and working individuals who want an offline personal ledger rather than a professional accounting system. Each account has its own user identifier. Shared system categories are available to all accounts, while custom categories belong to a particular user. The desktop stores several accounts locally, although only one account is represented by the current in-memory session at a time.
Objectives and boundaries

items.text: The system does not include bank synchronization, investment portfolios, tax filing, loan management, email delivery, web access or a remote REST backend. An allocation deposit changes goal balances independently of transaction cashflow. A payment mode is a text description, not a connection to a payment provider.

The repository supports a layered, incrementally extensible design. The MST presentation proposed Agile/Scrum and a 14-week plan; no sprint records, interview transcripts or retrospective minutes were provided. That plan is historical intent, not an independently verified development chronology.

items.text: Corrections to the MST architecture

MST slides 3 and 7 mention Spring/Hibernate, React, REST controllers and interchangeable server databases. Those technologies are not dependencies or runtime components of the inspected application. The final architecture is a JavaFX desktop process with ordinary Java method calls and JDBC DAOs. There are no FXML screen files despite the javafx-fxml dependency.

Slide 2 lists multi-user accounts out of scope, while slide 5 requires registration and sign-in. The final system resolves this tension by implementing multiple local accounts with one current session. It does not implement simultaneous remote multi-user service access. Slide 6 treats a database and automated scheduler as secondary actors; the final use-case boundary treats both as internal components.

The presentation groups functions under FR-01 through FR-08. Source comments use a different, more granular FR numbering, for example budgets as FR-06/07 and recommendations as FR-13. This report retains the original eight MST identifiers as its requirement baseline and records comment aliases explicitly. Additional documentation IDs EXT-01 through EXT-04 identify final features without silently renumbering the MST.
Constraints

The application depends on a compatible JavaFX runtime, available local files and a writable working directory. Recurring work does not execute while the process is closed; startup catch-up handles overdue occurrences. No response-time benchmark, concurrency capacity or formal security certification is claimed.
Source evidence: pom.xml; service/AuthService.java; app/MainApp.java; Finance_Analyzer_MST.pptx:slides 2,3,5,6,7
2.1 Use Cases
2.1.1 Use-Case Diagrams

The primary actor is the account holder. Before sign-in, the same person may create an account or submit credentials. After sign-in, the account identifier is passed to the controllers. Diagram boundaries represent the entire local application; SQLite and the recurring scheduler are not external actors.

items.caption: Figure 1. Account access and transaction tracking

items.text: Recording an entry includes validation; editing also validates the changed data. Deletion is confirmed rather than treated as a validation subcase. Searching and category creation are separate user goals. A successful account registration opens the same application shell as a successful login. No administrator or password-reset workflow is modeled because the source does not expose those capabilities.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/LoginController.java:handleAction(); ui/controllers/TransactionsController.java; service/TransactionService.java

items.caption: Figure 2. Planning, automation and analysis use cases

items.text: The planning use cases represent persisted budgets and goals. Creating or activating a goal checks the sum of active allocation ratios. Allocating a deposit is a separate operation; creating income does not automatically allocate savings. Managing a recurring rule configures future ledger generation rather than instructing a bank to debit funds.

Reports, charts and advice read saved records. The advice toggle and fixed-category selection are distinct preferences: disabling advice suppresses all rule messages; marking a category fixed excludes it only from discretionary concentration and category-spike checks. Snapshot creation and restore are exposed functions, but restore is partial and is not a complete account recovery contract.
Source evidence: service/GoalService.java:createGoal(),toggleGoalActive(); service/RatioAllocationService.java:allocateDeposit(); io/BackupManager.java:restoreBackup()
UC-01  Register, sign in and sign out
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-01
Preconditions: Application initialization completes; local database is reachable.
Trigger: Select Register & Sign In or Sign In.

Main success flow: 1. Enter username and password. 2. Validate registration fields or nonempty login input. 3. Registration checks duplicate username, hashes the password and saves User; login retrieves User and checks BCrypt. 4. Initialize default fixed-category preferences as needed. 5. Set currentUser and open the shell. 6. Sign Out clears currentUser and shows login.

Alternative flows and exceptions: Invalid fields or credentials produce an AuthenticationException message. Duplicate usernames are rejected. Database failures are not comprehensively caught by the login handler, so they remain a reliability risk. Canceling registration mode does not create an account.
Postconditions: A successful operation establishes one in-memory session. Password plaintext is not saved; logout does not delete stored records.
Source evidence: service/AuthService.java:register(),login(),logout(); dao/jdbc/JdbcUserDao.java:save()

Registration accepts at least six username characters from letters, digits, underscore, dot and hyphen; demo is a special accepted short name. Password validation requires at least six characters. These are implemented rules, not a recommendation that six-character passwords are sufficient for production security. Account deletion and credential recovery are not user-facing functions.
UC-02  Record income or expense
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-02, FR-07
Preconditions: Signed in; an appropriate category is available.
Trigger: Transactions > New Transaction.

Main success flow: 1. Choose Income or Expense. 2. Enter amount, category, date, payment mode and optional notes. 3. Observe live preview. 4. Save. 5. UI and service validation run. 6. Income goes through transactionDao.save(); expense uses direct JDBC in addExpense(). 7. Table reloads; dashboard/budgets reload on navigation.

Alternative flows and exceptions: Nonpositive amounts and scale above two decimal places are rejected. Expense dates after today are rejected. SQL insert failure reports an error; addExpense rolls back. Preview does not itself save any data.
Postconditions: A new persisted row has a generated ID, positive stored amount and explicit INCOME/EXPENSE type.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/TransactionDialogController.java:handleSave(); service/TransactionService.java:addIncome(),addExpense()
UC-03  Edit or delete a transaction
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-02
Preconditions: Signed in; selected row belongs to current account.
Trigger: Double-click row to edit or choose Delete Transaction.
Main success flow: Edit: open populated dialog, keep the type locked, change permitted fields, save and reload. Delete: request deletion, confirm, call deleteTransaction(id,userId), then reload.
Alternative flows and exceptions: Cancel closes without persistence. No selection produces a prompt. Failed updates/deletes may return false or raise a data-access exception.
Postconditions: Successful edit replaces stored values; successful delete removes the selected user-scoped row.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/TransactionsController.java:handleEditSelected(),handleDeleteSelected(); dao/jdbc/JdbcTransactionDao.java:update(),deleteById()
UC-04  Classify and find financial records
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-02, FR-03
Preconditions: Signed in; transaction list initialized.
Trigger: Add Category or apply Search & Filters.

Main success flow: Create a named category with income/expense type; reject an existing case-insensitive name. For retrieval, specify date range, category, type, amount bounds or notes/category keyword; execute user-scoped query and replace table data. Reset removes filters.

Alternative flows and exceptions: Blank or duplicate category names are rejected. Nonnumeric filter amounts currently become null rather than producing validation feedback. Custom category classification does not alter existing rows automatically.
Postconditions: A saved category becomes selectable; filtered results remain scoped to the account.
Source evidence: service/TransactionService.java:addCustomCategory(),findFiltered(); ui/controllers/TransactionsController.java:applyFilters()
UC-05  Manage monthly category budgets
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-04
Preconditions: Signed in; expense category and month selected.
Trigger: Budgets > Set Category Budget.

Main success flow: Enter a positive limit and save. Upsert the unique user/category/month record. Query spending in that category and month. Calculate utilization and show NORMAL, WARNING or EXCEEDED. Edit or delete through the row menu.
Alternative flows and exceptions: Zero/negative limits fail validation. Missing budget gives normal status in the alert service. Overspending is allowed; warnings do not block saving an expense.
Postconditions: A persisted monthly limit and calculated spending comparison are visible.
Source evidence: service/BudgetService.java:setBudget(),calculateUtilisation(); dao/jdbc/JdbcBudgetDao.java:save()
UC-06  Create, manage and fund savings goals
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-05, EXT-04
Preconditions: Signed in; current active-goal ratios are available.
Trigger: Savings Goals > New Savings Goal or Allocate Savings Deposit.

Main success flow: 1. Enter title, positive target, deadline and ratio from 0 to 100. 2. Validate fields and active ratio sum. 3. Save a new active goal. 4. Enter a positive deposit. 5. Read active goals and calculate each rounded share. 6. Batch saved_paise increments within one JDBC transaction. 7. Commit and show allocation summary.

Alternative flows and exceptions: Blank titles, nonpositive targets, missing/past deadlines or out-of-range ratios are rejected. The implementation accepts today as a deadline. Exceeding 100% active allocation raises AllocationRatioException. SQL failure rolls back allocation updates. Cancel performs no write.
Postconditions: Goal rows reflect saved allocations. Remainder is returned in the result but has no persisted unallocated-savings account.
Source evidence: service/GoalService.java:createGoal(),updateGoal(),toggleGoalActive(); service/RatioAllocationService.java:allocateDeposit()

Example expectation, not an executed database test: a INR 1,000 deposit with active ratios 60% and 30% yields INR 600 and INR 300, with INR 100 unallocated. Allocation does not reduce the transaction net cashflow. Progress display is capped at 100%, although saved amounts may exceed the target.

The New/Edit dialog uses a scrollable form and separate action footer. Its size is capped to the current screen bounds after showing. This code change addresses clipping; 100%, 125% and 150% scaling still require manual acceptance checks.
UC-07  Configure and process recurring transactions
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-06
Preconditions: Signed in to create rules; application process running to execute scheduled work.
Trigger: Create Rule, Run Catch-up Now, startup catch-up or periodic timer.

Main success flow: 1. Select type/category, positive amount, frequency and start date; end date is optional. 2. Save ACTIVE rule with nextDueDate=startDate. 3. Find active rules due on/before today. 4. Generate each missed occurrence. 5. Save audit message and advance date with Frequency.nextDate(). 6. Mark expired when the following date exceeds the end date.

Alternative flows and exceptions: End date before start is rejected. Paused rules are skipped until resumed. Processing failure is logged. The current save/audit/advance sequence is not one atomic database transaction, so a mid-sequence failure may cause duplicate retry records.
Postconditions: Transactions carry recurring_rule_id; rule stores its next date/status; execution history records success/failure.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/RecurringController.java:handleAddRule(),handleRunCatchUp(); service/RecurringScheduler.java:runCatchUp(),processRule()

items.caption: Table 4. Recurring intervals and persisted state
rows: Advance from the current occurrence using plusMonths(1) / plusYears(1).
Persisted RuleStatus enum values. No background service runs when app is closed.

items.text: The manual catch-up command calls the scheduler synchronously from the UI handler. Large backlogs can block interaction; no backlog performance measurement was performed. Automatic periodic callbacks use Platform.runLater to refresh UI tables.
UC-08  Review financial position and preferences
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: FR-08, EXT-01, EXT-03
Preconditions: Signed in; saved records may be empty.
Trigger: Open Dashboard or refresh monthly report; change advice/fixed preferences.

Main success flow: Read income, expense and category totals. Construct charts and goal snapshot. Build AnalysisContext and evaluate five rules when enabled. Generate monthly text with category/budget/goal summaries. Persist preference changes and refresh insight display after successful advice update.

Alternative flows and exceptions: Zero income avoids division by zero. Disabled advice produces no messages. Individual rule exceptions are logged and do not stop all other rules. Historical micro-spend advice is not strictly aligned to the selected report month.
Postconditions: A read-only analysis is displayed; only explicitly changed preferences are saved.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/DashboardController.java:refreshView(); service/ReportService.java:generateMonthlyReportText(); service/HeuristicEngine.java:generateRecommendations()
UC-09  Transfer financial data through files
Primary actor: Account holder
Requirements: EXT-02
Preconditions: Signed in; suitable file path selected.
Trigger: Reports & Settings file button.

Main success flow: Export writes CSV or text; import validates CSV rows and counts imported/skipped records. Backup serializes UserDataSnapshot. Restore reads snapshot and appends selected records to the current account.

Alternative flows and exceptions: Canceling file selection performs no operation. Invalid rows are skipped with reasons. Restore omits recurring rules/preferences, may duplicate records and is not atomic as a whole.
Postconditions: Selected output file exists after successful export; imported records persist where accepted. Restore is only a partial import, not exact recovery.
Source evidence: io/CsvImporter.java; io/CsvExporter.java; io/BackupManager.java

items.caption: Figure 3. Expense entry with validation and persistence

items.text: The activity starts when the account holder opens a new transaction dialog. The amount and category listeners calculate an advisory preview while the record remains unsaved. Save triggers explicit field parsing and validation. The expense service checks the selected category and rejects an invalid amount or future date.

The expense insertion is protected by setAutoCommit(false), commit and rollback. Generated keys populate the object identifier. Only the success path closes the dialog and refreshes the transaction table. Returning to Dashboard or Budgets calls the navigation refresh callbacks. These activities do not imply a bank transaction or automatic savings-goal deduction.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/TransactionDialogController.java:triggerPreviewUpdate(),handleSave(); service/TransactionService.java:addExpense()

items.caption: Figure 4. Goal creation followed by ratio allocation

items.text: Goal creation and funding are separate actions. Validation checks the new ratio against the total of currently active goals. A new goal begins active with zero saved amount. A deposit then uses the current active set to calculate shares and applies all saved-balance changes inside a JDBC transaction.

An inactive goal receives no new allocation. The remainder reported to the user is a calculated result, not an account balance in the schema. Independent per-goal rounding can over-allocate tiny deposits; this is a known limitation rather than an omitted decision state. A target being reached is not an automatic transition to inactive: active status is explicitly changed by the user.
Source evidence: service/GoalService.java:createGoal(); service/RatioAllocationService.java:allocateDeposit(); model/SavingsGoal.java:getProgressPercentage()

items.caption: Figure 5. Responsibilities across user, interface, logic and persistence

items.text: The swimlanes separate responsibility rather than imply remote services. The user supplies information; JavaFX controls collect it; the transaction service enforces validation; JDBC reads categories and inserts the expense. These operations occur in the local process. There is no HTTP request, REST controller, ORM session or server-side deployment.

The diagram intentionally shows direct expense SQL under persistence while naming TransactionService as its caller. addExpense() contains that SQL itself; it does not delegate to JdbcTransactionDao.save(). Income creation does use the DAO save method. Acknowledging this asymmetry is more accurate than presenting a perfectly uniform architecture that the code does not implement.
Source evidence: service/TransactionService.java:addIncome(),addExpense(); ui/controllers/TransactionsController.java:handleAddTransaction()
2.3.1 DFD Level 0

items.caption: Figure 6. Context diagram with external entities and data flows

items.text: The context boundary includes authentication, financial records, analytics, scheduled processing and persistence. The external account holder exchanges credentials, entry data, plan settings, queries and preferences with the application. A user-selected file is a separate external source/sink for CSV, report text and serialized snapshots.

DFD notation is data-oriented: rectangles are external entities, circles are transformations, arrows carry named data, and parallel-rule stores appear only in decomposed levels. An arrow is not a method call or execution-order edge. The context diagram deliberately excludes a database actor because SQLite is inside the system boundary.

The aggregated user-input flow is decomposed at Level 1 into credentials, tracking details, planning settings, analysis queries/preferences and file-operation queries. Outputs are decomposed into authentication/operation results, record views, previews, charts/advice and reports. File inputs and outputs retain the same logical content across levels.
Source evidence: app/MainApp.java:showMainShell(); ui/controllers/ReportsSettingsController.java; io/UserDataSnapshot.java

items.caption: Figure 7. Major transformations and logical stores

items.text: Processes 1.0-5.0 divide authentication, tracking, planning, analysis/reporting and file transfer. D1 groups account/preference tables; D2 groups category, transaction and recurring data; D3 groups budgets and savings goals. Repeated symbols identify the same external account holder and logical stores, not extra users or databases.

The same account-holder and file exchanges from Level 0 remain at Level 1. File-operation query is a decomposition of the context query input. Internal report text passes from analysis to transfer for text export. Internal scheduled generation belongs to tracking and is not represented as a new external user input. DFDs describe the implemented data responsibilities, including partial restore; they do not assert atomicity of all process writes.
Source evidence: dao/jdbc/DatabaseManager.java:initializeDatabase(); service/ReportService.java; io/BackupManager.java

items.caption: Figure 8. Decomposition of tracking process 2.0

items.text: This diagram expands only process 2.0. Transaction details enter validation, valid entries reach persistence, queries reach retrieval, and category/rule settings reach their management transformation. The D2 interface retains stored-record reads and record-change writes. The external outputs remain operation results and record views.

A validation result is one kind of operation result, not an additional context-level output. The diagram does not add budget-preview inputs to process 2.0 because previews belong to analysis process 4.0 at Level 1. This separation keeps the parent and child interfaces balanced. In the actual UI both responsibilities are combined in the transaction dialog.
The official contents repeat number 2.3.2 for Level 2. The numbering here is corrected to 2.3.3 while preserving the required hierarchy and all three DFD levels.
Source evidence: service/TransactionService.java; ui/controllers/RecurringController.java; dao/jdbc/JdbcTransactionDao.java

title: 2.4 Software Requirement Specification in IEEE Format

items.text: Introduction, purpose and scope

This SRS uses an IEEE 830-style organization: introduction, overall description, specific requirements, external interfaces and verification traceability. It is a structured academic SRS, not a claim of certification against a standard. Its purpose is to specify the delivered local desktop behavior and identify verification gaps before acceptance.

The product boundary is one JavaFX application process and its local data files. Its principal functions are manual ledger management, financial planning and interpretable analysis. Requirements below describe implemented behavior unless explicitly labeled target or proposed. Evidence is differentiated as code inspection, executed automated test, historical runtime log or not executed.

items.text: Overall description

The intended user understands dates, categories and monetary amounts but need not know SQL or Java. Java 21 and JavaFX are required for execution. Maven resolves and launches development builds. The data path is relative to the working directory, so demonstrations should launch from the repository root. The desktop and operating-system clock supply dates and recurring scheduling context.

items.text: Acceptance boundaries

FR-01 does not include forgotten-password recovery, email verification or server authentication. Usernames accept a restricted character set with a demo exception. Password strength beyond minimum length is not enforced. Financial-data separation primarily relies on user-scoped UI queries and updates; not every DAO lookup takes a user ID.

FR-02 accepts descriptive payment modes, optional notes and date/category/type/amount/keyword filters. Invalid amount-filter text currently disables that bound rather than producing a warning. Future income dates are not rejected by the income validator. Budget warnings are informational; overspending is not blocked.

FR-03 categories have a type and may be system-wide or account-specific. The final interface supports category creation, not a general category editing/deletion screen. FR-04 limits are unique per user/category/month; setting an existing combination updates the limit through SQL upsert.
Source evidence: service/AuthService.java; util/Validators.java; ui/controllers/TransactionsController.java:parseBigDecimal(); dao/jdbc/JdbcBudgetDao.java:save()

items.text: Calculation and timing semantics

FR-05 deposit allocation is a bookkeeping update to goal balances. It neither checks available net income nor debits an account. Independent rounding is a limitation for tiny deposits. Target completion changes a derived progress value, not a stored lifecycle state.

FR-06 supports DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY and YEARLY. Periodic checks default to five minutes. The process must be running; startup catch-up iterates missed dates. No exactly-once execution guarantee is asserted because transaction insert, audit insert and next-date update are separate operations.

FR-07 is implemented for the current month using an additive proposed amount. A new current-month entry is its reliable intended case. Editing and backdating do not have replacement-aware/date-aware previews. FR-08 report totals use the selected month, but micro-spend advice uses a recent list and today-based window; historical advice therefore has a known period mismatch.
Source evidence: service/RatioAllocationService.java; service/RecurringScheduler.java; service/DefaultInModalAnalyticsService.java; rules/FrequentMicroTransactionsRule.java

items.text: DatabaseManager enables PRAGMA foreign_keys on each connection. Transaction dates and year-month values are stored as text and selected using an ISO month prefix. User-related rows generally cascade when a user is deleted at DAO level, although the UI does not offer account deletion. Deleting a recurring rule sets existing transaction recurring_rule_id values to NULL and cascades its execution audit rows.

The relational references support one user to many transactions, budgets and goals, and one category to many transactions. A system category may have no owning user. Java domain objects store foreign-key identifiers rather than direct nested User/Category object references. The schema does not encode the cross-row active-ratio total; GoalService enforces it in application logic.
Source evidence: dao/jdbc/DatabaseManager.java:initializeDatabase(),getConnection(); dao/jdbc/JdbcTransactionDao.java:getTotalExpenseInMonth()

title: SRS interfaces, security and financial logic

items.text: External interface requirements

The user interface is local JavaFX: Login/Register, Dashboard, Transactions, Budgets, Savings Goals, Recurring Rules, and Reports & Settings. Modal dialogs collect transaction, budget, goal, allocation and recurring details. No network protocol or REST interface is required. Software interfaces are JDBC, JavaFX lifecycle/events, BCrypt, Java logging and file streams.

CSV exchange uses Date,Type,Category,Amount,PaymentMode,Notes with ISO dates and decimal rupee amounts. Imports process one line at a time, skip malformed records, and expose imported/skipped counts. Text reports use a file chooser. Binary snapshots use Java object serialization, contain financial data and a User object including its password hash, and are not encrypted.

items.caption: Table 11. Financial logic and acceptance examples
rows: Income - expense; (income - expense)/income x 100. INR 50,000 and INR 1,100 imply INR 48,900 and 97.8%.
(spent + proposed expense)/limit x 100. INR 1,000 against INR 1,200 implies about 83.33%.
Deposit x ratio/100 rounded to two decimals; 60% of INR 1,000 is INR 600.
Flexible category amount / (all expenses - fixed expenses); trigger strictly above 40%.
Expense/income >90%; net savings/income <10%; category growth >=25% with prior >=INR 500; >=5 expenses below INR 200.

items.text: Security limitations include a plain local SQLite file, a publicly advertised demo account and unrestricted Java snapshot deserialization. Snapshots should be treated as trusted local files. No independent security audit, encrypted storage, remote role management or simultaneous-user isolation guarantee is claimed. Numerical examples above are expected calculations, not database executions.
Source evidence: io/CsvExporter.java; io/CsvImporter.java; io/UserDataSnapshot.java; rules/*Rule.java; util/MoneyUtil.java

Implementation status is established by connected code paths, not button presence. Current GUI operations and database integration cases are not certified by inspection. Full repository-relative paths and method locations are supplied in REQUIREMENTS_TRACEABILITY.md and evidence/source_index.json.

3.1 Class Diagram
Case 1 Transaction management

items.caption: Figure 9. Actual transaction classes, interfaces and dependencies

items.text: Income and Expense inherit the shared identifiers, amount, date and descriptive fields of abstract Transaction. Their getType() and getSignedAmount() methods supply dynamic behavior. JdbcTransactionDao realizes TransactionDao, whose generic parent contract is Dao<Transaction,Long>. Dashed dependencies indicate service use or object construction, not ownership.

Multiplicity between Transaction and Category is a relational identifier reference: each saved transaction has one category_id and a category may classify many transactions. It is not a Java field of type Category. TransactionService validates category existence before saving. Its expense path contains direct JDBC SQL, while its income path calls the DAO interface. The diagram therefore shows both object creation and persistence abstraction without claiming uniform delegation.
Source evidence: model/Transaction.java; model/Income.java; model/Expense.java; dao/TransactionDao.java; service/TransactionService.java

items.caption: Figure 10. Planning services and financial models

items.text: BudgetService creates monthly Budget objects and delegates storage to BudgetDao. GoalService creates and validates SavingsGoal objects using SavingsGoalDao. RatioAllocationService reads active goals through that interface but executes its allocation batch directly using DatabaseManager. That direct SQL dependency is explained in the component model.

The userId fields represent one account to many budgets or goals through foreign keys. User is omitted from this focused service view; no owning List<Budget> or List<SavingsGoal> is present in that Java model. The stored active flag is separate from progress. A goal remains active after reaching its target unless explicitly deactivated. Dashed dependencies indicate service use, not ownership.
Source evidence: model/Budget.java; model/SavingsGoal.java; service/GoalService.java; service/RatioAllocationService.java; dao/SavingsGoalDao.java
Case 1 Adding an expense

items.caption: Figure 11. Expense validation and JDBC commit sequence

items.text: The participant named TransactionDialog represents TransactionDialogController. Validators.validateExpense() is invoked by TransactionService; the self-call summarizes a static utility invocation rather than a separate remote component. The JDBC/SQLite participant combines the connection, statement and database for readability.

On SQLException the insert path calls rollback() and throws DataAccessException; the dialog catches the exception and keeps the form available. The success result is an Expense with its generated ID. TransactionsController then re-queries the table. Preview queries occur before this save sequence and do not commit a record. No JdbcTransactionDao.save() call is inserted into the expense sequence because it is absent from addExpense().
Source evidence: ui/controllers/TransactionDialogController.java:handleSave(); service/TransactionService.java:addExpense()
Case 2 Creating a savings goal

items.caption: Figure 12. Goal validation, ratio check and insertion

items.text: GoalService validates the proposed fields, reads all active goals and sums allocation ratios before insertion. If the total plus the new ratio exceeds 100, AllocationRatioException is raised before save(). JdbcSavingsGoalDao binds values to INSERT savings_goals and returns the object with a generated identifier.

The sequence documents creation only. Funding is a later RatioAllocationService operation, not a side effect of createGoal(). Validation and the sum check are application operations; they are not a database-wide cross-row constraint or a proven concurrent transaction guarantee. The dialog catches ratio errors separately and presents a targeted warning.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/GoalsController.java:handleAddOrEditGoal(); service/GoalService.java:createGoal(); dao/jdbc/JdbcSavingsGoalDao.java:save()
Case 1 Transaction persistence

items.caption: Figure 13. Numbered expense-persistence object messages

items.text: This communication diagram emphasizes object links and numbered messages rather than time-scaled lifelines. Message 1 starts the use case, 1.1 obtains category information, 1.2 validates fields, and 1.3-1.6 perform transactional JDBC work. The dashed return completes the Expense result.

The local JDBC Connection and database are represented separately to expose the persistence boundary. prepareStatement() creates a PreparedStatement, which is abbreviated into the connection interaction to avoid overcrowding. executeUpdate() inserts one row; generated-key retrieval assigns the ID. The commit/rollback label represents alternative outcomes and does not imply both execute on success.

Income persistence uses transactionDao.save() instead of the direct expense SQL path. The collaboration is intentionally limited to one significant actual scenario rather than merging incompatible alternatives into a single call chain.
Source evidence: service/TransactionService.java:addExpense(); dao/jdbc/DatabaseManager.java:getConnection()
Case 2 Financial recommendation generation

items.caption: Figure 14. Recommendation engine and rule communication

items.text: DashboardController queries current and previous spending before passing AnalysisContext to HeuristicEngine. The engine checks the user preference, obtains account-specific fixed-category information through CategoryService, and creates an enriched context using withFixedCategoryData(). It iterates over five Recommendation implementations and collects present Optional<String> messages.

Message 1.4* indicates repetition over rules. Each rule can return empty rather than an error when no condition is met. The engine catches exceptions from individual evaluations and logs them; advice from other rules can still be collected. Recommendation has two abstract methods, evaluate() and getRuleName(), so it is not a Java functional interface despite an inaccurate source comment.

HighCategorySpendRule and CategorySpikeRule skip fixed categories. Total-expense and savings-rate rules still include fixed obligations. The communication therefore supports explainable advice without suggesting a machine-learning model or external recommendation service.
Source evidence: service/HeuristicEngine.java:generateRecommendations(); rules/Recommendation.java; rules/AnalysisContext.java:withFixedCategoryData()
Case 1 Transaction dialog lifecycle

items.caption: Figure 15. Conceptual transaction-dialog states

items.text: These are conceptual UI workflow states, not values stored in transactions. A new form permits a type choice; an edit form starts from an existing object and disables type controls. Both enter validation on Save. Invalid input or an SQL error leaves the dialog available for correction.

Successful persistence closes the dialog and returns saved=true. Cancel closes without a persistence call. A database transaction does not have a stored DRAFT, APPROVED or POSTED status in this schema. Those states would be invented domain behavior and are intentionally absent. The form can mutate an existing in-memory object before a failed update, which is a known implementation boundary rather than a separately persisted state.
Source evidence: ui/controllers/TransactionDialogController.java:showAndWait(),handleSave(); dao/jdbc/DatabaseManager.java:transactions schema
Case 2 Persisted active status of a goal

items.caption: Figure 16. Savings-goal active flag and deletion

items.text: The stored state distinction is is_active=1 or is_active=0. A valid creation starts active. Deactivation removes the goal from future allocation; reactivation checks whether its ratio fits within the current active pool. Deletion removes the row rather than changing a status to DELETED.

Funding changes saved_paise while retaining the active flag. Reaching the target does not automatically deactivate a goal. getProgressPercentage() derives a percentage and caps its display at 100. A deadline passing is not an implemented EXPIRED transition for SavingsGoal. Recurring rules have a separate ACTIVE/PAUSED/EXPIRED enumeration and must not be confused with goal states.
This distinction between persisted state and derived display prevents a common design-document error: representing desirable lifecycle transitions that the application never performs.
Source evidence: service/GoalService.java:toggleGoalActive(),deleteGoal(); model/SavingsGoal.java:getProgressPercentage(); dao/jdbc/JdbcSavingsGoalDao.java:updateActiveStatus()
4.1 Component Diagrams

items.caption: Figure 17. Implemented application components and dependencies

items.text: MainApp constructs DAOs, services, file managers and controllers using constructor injection. JavaFX controllers combine view building and event handling. Services implement business rules, while JDBC DAOs map rows to models. HeuristicEngine coordinates the independent Recommendation implementations. RecurringScheduler owns a single-thread scheduled executor.

The component structure is layered but not perfectly strict: DashboardController queries DAOs directly; TransactionService.addExpense() and RatioAllocationService.allocateDeposit() contain direct SQL; MainApp wires file-operation callbacks. These exceptions are visible rather than concealed by an invented web MVC architecture. MainApp.stop() shuts down the scheduler and logger.

Java language mechanisms include abstract classes, interfaces, overriding, overloaded constructors/methods, generic DAOs, collections, lambdas, streams, try-with-resources and checked/unchecked exceptions. Transaction.getSignedAmount() is overridden by Income and Expense; AnalysisContext.isFixed(long/String) is an actual overload.
Source evidence: app/MainApp.java:init(),showMainShell(),stop(); model/Transaction.java; rules/AnalysisContext.java

items.caption: Figure 18. Single-device Java desktop deployment

items.text: The executable environment is a local Java 21 JVM with JavaFX and JDBC libraries. Maven is a build/launch tool, not a hosted runtime service. The application accesses data/finance.db through a local SQLite JDBC URL and loads app.properties/style.css as resources. File choosers write CSV, text and snapshots to user-selected paths.

There is no deployed React frontend, Spring Boot server, REST endpoint, MySQL/PostgreSQL service or cloud component. JavaFX native libraries must match the platform. The repository JAR configuration is not a standalone installer or a verified bundled runtime distribution; the supported development launch path is Maven javafx:run from the repository directory.

Because the database path is relative, changing the working directory can select or create a different database. The report build does not launch the app or initialize its database. RecurringScheduler.start() performs immediate catch-up, so capturing future screenshots should use an isolated demonstration copy if existing records must remain unchanged.
Source evidence: pom.xml:javafx-maven-plugin; src/main/resources/app.properties; app/Launcher.java; service/RecurringScheduler.java:start()

5.1 Test Plan

The test objective is to establish confidence in financial validation, calculation and persistence while distinguishing code inspection from executed behavior. The report preparation compiled production and test sources in a temporary directory and ran only existing database-free tests. It did not initialize or change the production SQLite file. The test run is dated 16 November 2026.

The strategy combines white-box inspection of validation/transaction boundaries with boundary-value and equivalence-class tests. Amount classes are null, zero, negative, valid two-decimal and excessive scale. Budget boundaries are below 80%, at 80%, below 100% and at/above 100%. Goal ratios test within and above the 100% active pool. Planned GUI cases cover navigation refresh, type lock, advice toggle and goal-dialog scaling.

items.text: Completion and acceptance boundary

The documented application is a local Java desktop prototype with substantial tracking, planning and analysis functionality. Production and test source compilation and a selected 18-method automated run provide limited objective evidence. Final submission still requires genuine screenshots, filled cover details, manual scaling checks, and peer results if the course requires them.
